summary: STORM-inspired verified research: crisis/self-harm handling policy for an AI career counsellor serving Indian minors

result.topic: How should an AI study-abroad and career-guidance counsellor serving Indian students (many aged 13-18, i.e. minors) handle disclosures of distress, self-harm or suicidal thoughts in chat or voice, so the student gets the safest possible help while the operating company and its human counsellors carry minimum legal liability?

roster.name: Indian Law and Regulation
roster.mandate: Map what Indian law requires and permits for an AI counsellor serving minors: Mental Healthcare Act 2017 s.115 (attempted suicide presumed under severe stress, not punishable) and minor-treatment provisions, DPDP Act 2023 and 2025 Rules (verifiable parental consent for under-18s, exemptions, what counts as a crisis-data lawful basis), POCSO s.19/21 mandatory reporting when a disclosure involves sexual abuse, IT Rules 2021 intermediary duties, and NCPCR/MoE school guidance. Flag where final rule text still needs checking against the Gazette.
roster.source: https://www.medianama.com/2025/01/223-data-protection-rules-2025-children-data-india/ (DPDP children's-data rules; search surfaced the 18-month transition window, Rule 10 verification and exemptions; MHCA s.115 and POCSO s.19 returned no results and need a follow-up search)

roster.name: Clinical Safe-Messaging and Crisis Practice
roster.mandate: Define the clinically sound response to distress, self-harm and suicidal ideation in text and voice for adolescents: WHO and AFSP safe-messaging rules (no method detail, no glamourisation), risk-tier triage, warm handoff over cold referral, and Indian crisis routes (Tele-MANAS 14416, KIRAN, iCall, Vandrevala, 112), adapted from the 988 and Tele-MANAS protocols. Cover tone, language (Hindi/Hinglish/regional), and what the bot must never do (diagnose, promise confidentiality, act as therapist).
roster.source: Mandated by the task brief (b); WHO, AFSP and Tele-MANAS primary documents to be retrieved by the researcher

roster.name: AI Chat Product Practice and US Companion-Chatbot Law
roster.mandate: Benchmark how deployed AI products handle minors in crisis, and what recent litigation and US statute now demand: OpenAI ChatGPT teen safeguards and parental controls, Character.AI lawsuits and its under-18 changes, Replika, Snapchat My AI, Woebot and Wysa, plus California SB 243 (in force 1 Jan 2026: published suicide-prevention protocol, crisis referral, AI disclosure, break reminders every 3 hours for known minors, annual reporting to the Office of Suicide Prevention, private right of action with $1,000 per violation minimum) and New York's companion-chatbot law. Extract transferable design patterns and the failure modes that produced liability.
roster.source: https://natlawreview.com/article/ai-regulatory-update-californias-sb-243-mandates-companion-ai-safety-and (California SB 243 requirements and enforcement; also https://agora.eto.tech/instrument/4944)

roster.name: Liability, Duty of Care and False-Positive Skeptic
roster.mandate: Stress-test the premise that the company and its human counsellors can carry 'minimum' liability while giving the safest help. Examine duty of care once risk is detected, negligence exposure from both missed detections and over-escalation, human-in-the-loop escalation (who is reachable, when, and what happens at 2am), false-positive harm (unnecessary parent or school disclosure, loss of student trust, chilling disclosure), confidentiality versus parental-notification conflicts, and where disclaimers and terms of service fail to shield a company. Argue that safety and liability minimisation sometimes conflict, and say which should win.
roster.source: Mandated by the task brief (d); builds on the SB 243 private right of action and the gap noted in search results that no duty-of-care framing was found, so a follow-up search is needed

roster.name: Indian Youth-Counselling Ground Reality
roster.mandate: Practitioner view from the field: how school counsellors, helpline responders and study-abroad advisers in India actually meet adolescent distress. Cover family and exam-pressure stressors, stigma and fear of parental disclosure, student-counsellor-parent-school trust triangles, voice and vernacular code-switching, and workable human-escalation staffing and training in an edtech or study-abroad setting. Turn the legal, clinical and industry findings into an operational playbook a small counselling team could run.
roster.source: Replaces the generic practitioner lens with a topic-specific one; evidence to be gathered from Tele-MANAS, NCPCR and school-counselling field reports

findings.claim: MHCA 2017 s.115 protects the student, not the operator. A person who attempts suicide is presumed to be under severe stress and cannot be tried and punished under the IPC. The State, not a private AI company, carries the duty to provide care, treatment and rehabilitation. So a distress disclosure creates no criminal exposure for the student. The Act also gives the company no safe harbour and creates no legal duty for the company to treat. Caveat: I fetched s.115 text only from SCC Times quoting the Act, not from India Code (the official PDF returned 403), so check it against the Gazette. A Supreme Court notice on the provision's validity appeared in search snippets that I did not fetch, so I report it as unverified.

The DPDP Act makes parental consent the default for all chat or voice data from under-18s, and a distress disclosure is personal data like any other. The Act requires verifiable parental consent before any processing of a child's data. Rule 10 requires the fiduciary to check that the person claiming to be the parent is an adult. 'Adult' means 18 or older. The Act also bars tracking or behavioural monitoring of children. A risk-scoring or distress-flagging pipeline that profiles a minor's messages over time could be argued to be 'behavioural monitoring' (my inference, with no case law found). Section 9(2) separately bars processing likely to harm a child's well-being.

The DPDP child-data exemptions (Rule 12 and the Fourth Schedule) are narrow and probably do not cover a study-abroad and career counsellor. Part A exempts clinical or mental health establishments and healthcare professionals, but only for providing health services to the child and only as far as needed to protect her health. Educational institutions are exempt only for tracking and behavioural monitoring for educational activities or the safety of enrolled children. An AI study-abroad counsellor operated by a company is neither a mental health establishment nor an educational institution. Any exemption would have to be claimed through a clinical or school partner, or avoided by obtaining parental consent. Lawful basis: the only crisis-relevant 'legitimate use' without consent is s.7(f), a medical emergency 'involving a threat to the life or immediate threat to the health' of the person. It is limited to emergency response, not routine monitoring. No decided case applies it to an AI chat, so I treat any such use as untested. The Fourth Schedule text came from a third-party site (dpdprules.org) because the MeitY PDF returned 403, so verify it against the Gazette. A corrigendum has already relettered the Note items.

DPDP timing: the Rules are not yet in force on the operative provisions as of 16 Oct 2026. Rules 1, 2 and 17-21 took effect on 13 Nov 2025. Rule 4 (consent managers) takes effect on 13 Nov 2026. Rules 3, 5-16 (including Rule 10 on parental consent and Rule 12 on exemptions) and 22-23 take effect 18 months after publication, about 13 May 2027. The Fourth Schedule has no explicit commencement line, and one commentator computes 13 May 2027 and says the date is provisional. A search found that MeitY consulted in Jan 2026 on shortening these timelines, but it did not confirm that an amendment was notified. Flag for Gazette check: any timeline-compression notification, the exact publication date (13 vs 14 Nov 2025), and the Fourth Schedule's commencement. Design implication: build to the 2027 standard now, because the consent architecture takes longer to build than the grace period lasts.

POCSO is the one place where Indian law overrides confidentiality and privacy. A disclosure of sexual abuse by a minor triggers a reporting duty on 'any person', with no carve-out for counsellors, companies or consent. The report goes to the Special Juvenile Police Unit or local police, not to a parent. Failure carries up to 6 months' imprisonment or a fine. A person in charge of a company or institution who fails to report in respect of a subordinate under his control faces up to 1 year and a fine. Good-faith reporters have immunity from civil and criminal liability (s.19(7)). A July 2026 Supreme Court ruling (Linda Sema v State of Arunachal Pradesh), reported only through a law-firm blog that I could not check against the judgment, reportedly held that a school official cannot substitute a private inquiry for the police complaint and need not verify a child's account first. Unresolved, and my inference: whether the company 'knows' when only the AI has processed the chat, versus when a human counsellor reads it. Design logic: once any human at the operator reads such a transcript, the duty attaches to them and to the person in charge. The system must therefore route these flags to a trained human for s.19 reporting rather than leave them buried in logs. The POCSO text came from vidhijudicial.com and courtbook.in (not official), so confirm s.19 and s.21 against India Code.

The MHCA treats minor mental-health treatment as a parent or nominated-representative matter, which shows where the AI counsellor's role boundary sits. Under s.87, a minor can be admitted to a mental health establishment only through a prescribed procedure that starts with the nominated representative. Treatment of a minor needs the informed consent of the nominated representative. This governs admission and treatment in mental health establishments, not a chat advisory product. My inference is that an AI study-abroad counsellor that stays out of diagnosis and treatment, and only offers support, referral and escalation, is the safest legal posture. If it behaves like treatment, it risks drifting into licensed-practice territory. I did not find a statutory definition that places AI counselling in or out of 'mental health professional', so that is a gap to check. The s.87 text came from advocatekhoj.com, not India Code.

The operator's real criminal exposure is abetment, not s.115. BNS s.107 makes abetting the suicide of a child punishable by death, life imprisonment or up to 10 years. If the AI's output encouraged, instructed or facilitated self-harm, a prosecutor could frame the operator's people or design decisions as abetment. This is my inference. I found no case applying it to an AI system. Section 115 MHCA protects the person who attempts, not third parties. The practical safety and liability goals therefore align: blocking method or encouragement content and escalating to humans is both the safest help and the best defence. The BNS text came from lawx.in, not the Gazette, so verify it.

IT Rules 2021 / s.79 safe harbour is unreliable for an AI counsellor, so liability planning should not assume it. MeitY told the Lok Sabha on 29 July 2026 that whether an AI system is an intermediary depends on the nature of the service and the functions it performs. Section 79 protection needs the intermediary not to have initiated the transmission, selected the receiver, or modified the content, and generative output is arguably created by the operator rather than hosted for a user. This is commentary, with no court ruling found. I did not fetch the operative text of IT Rules 2021 rule 3. The tentative conclusion is that an AI chat counsellor should be treated as a first-party publisher of its own outputs, which makes its own duty of care and its guardrails the controlling factor. Flag: pending draft Second Amendment Rules would link safe harbour to MeitY advisories, and their final status needs Gazette verification.

The Supreme Court's July 2025 Sukdeb Saha guidelines, plus a verified helpline, set the de facto standard of care for student-facing support in India. The guidelines are binding on educational institutions under Article 141 and apply until a statute is enacted. They require a trained counsellor, psychologist or social worker for institutions above 100 students, prominently displayed helplines including Tele-MANAS, referral linkages for smaller institutions, and biannual staff training in psychological first aid. They bind schools and coaching centres, not a private AI company directly, but partner schools will demand compliance and a court is likely to treat them as the reference standard. This is my inference. Helpline verified on an official page: DGHS lists Tele-MANAS as 1800-89-14416 (short code 14416), 24x7. PIB pages returned 403, and secondary sources also give 1-800-891-4416, so confirm the exact string on telemanas.mohfw.gov.in before hard-coding it. NCPCR and MoE School Safety Guidelines 2021 and UMMEED text were not retrieved, so those are flagged as unchecked.

Safe-messaging for a counselling bot should be adapted from media-reporting guidance, which is the only formal 'safe messaging' corpus (WHO/IASP, AFSP-endorsed reportingonsuicide). Core rules: never describe method detail, do not sensationalise, always give a crisis number, use non-stigmatising language ('died by suicide', not 'successful/failed attempt'). Caveat: these were written for journalists, not 1:1 conversational agents, so applying them to a chatbot is an extrapolation. Also, I could not retrieve the WHO Dos and Don'ts text itself (403/overview only); the verbatim rule wording below comes from the Be The 1 To (Reporting on Suicide) page, and WHO's rationale from the WHO overview and fact sheet.

The Indian crisis route is Tele-MANAS 14416: a toll-free, 24/7, multilingual national line with a counsellor tier and a specialist tier (DMHP/medical college, e-Sanjeevani video), coordinated by NIMHANS. The latest official count (Lok Sabha reply, Feb 2026, via a search-result summary of the PIB page) is 53 cells in 36 States/UTs and 20 languages chosen by states, so language coverage varies by state. Not verified: PIB and mohfw pages returned 403 and the telemanas portal returned only its title when fetched, so the 14416 quote comes from an IIIT-Bangalore reproduction of the PIB launch text. Also unverified: KIRAN 1800-599-0019 (reported merged into Tele-MANAS, source page would not load) and Vandrevala (not searched); do not hard-code those numbers without confirming on official pages. 112 was not verified in this research.

iCall (TISS) is not a 24/7 line: official TISS page lists telephone counselling only Monday to Saturday 8 AM to 10 PM, with the number 022-25521111. iCall's own site shows the older 9152987821 number inconsistently flagged as unavailable. The bot's routing table must therefore carry hours per resource and never present a daytime-only line as the crisis route; Tele-MANAS is the 24/7 default. Caveat: language coverage of iCall was not confirmed on the TISS page.

Triage and handoff design: a tiered youth pathway (brief screen, then brief safety assessment by a trained clinician, then disposition) is the validated model, and it shows the bot's role is the screening/bridging tier, not assessment or treatment. NIMH ASQ: a 'yes' to any of four questions identified 97% of youth; screening is best done away from parents. The Stanley-Brown Safety Plan gives the structure for a warm handoff: warning signs, internal coping, social contacts as distraction, family/friends to help, professionals/crisis lines, means-safety, reasons for living. Caveat: the safety-plan page I fetched offers only testimonials, not trial data, and the ASQ toolkit is validated for medical settings with a clinician present, not for unattended chat, so porting it is untested. (The 988 call-flow could not be verified from an official page; only secondary sources came back, so I do not cite them.)

Means restriction belongs in the bot's script and is a place where general-purpose LLMs fail: WHO lists limiting access to means as a core evidence-based intervention, and Harvard Means Matter reports most attempt survivors do not later die by suicide. A RAND/Psychiatric Services study (Aug 2025) found chatbots refuse very-high-risk questions but are inconsistent at intermediate risk, and ChatGPT and Claude sometimes answered which methods have the highest completion rate. Design implication: hard-code refusal of method/lethality information at every risk tier, and test the middle band specifically. Caveat: the RAND figures are from a secondary summary (Psychiatric News alert), not the paper itself, and tested US-English prompts only; behaviour in Hindi/Hinglish is unmeasured.

What the bot must never do, from the youth-suicide-prevention sector: never act as therapist or crisis counsellor; always interrupt and redirect to real help on self-harm content every time; safeguards must not degrade over long sessions; never coach secrecy or push a minor to hide suicidal thoughts from trusted adults; build pathways to human care. Jed Foundation goes further and says no emotionally responsive chatbot should be offered to under-18s with age gates that cannot rely on self-reported birthdays, which directly challenges the premise of a minor-facing bot and should be flagged to the council as a minority/maximalist position, not consensus. Caveat: this is a US advocacy letter, not a regulation; Indian law was not checked for chatbot-specific rules.

Confidentiality is where clinical practice and liability collide, and where consensus is arguably wrong for India: Indian adolescents avoid counsellors mainly because they fear disclosures will reach parents; stigma is the top barrier; and a CHI study of Indian teens found 69% prefer text over 7% voice and that a US-only helpline was useless to them. So the bot must not promise confidentiality it cannot keep (the clinically honest line is a limited-confidentiality statement up front, with a safety exception), yet an over-eager 'we will tell your parents' script will drive disclosure away. Also, the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 s.115 presumes a person who attempts suicide to be under severe stress and bars trial/punishment, and obliges government to provide care, so the legal framing is care not criminality; this reduces fear of criminal exposure for disclosure but does not itself create a duty on the company. Caveat: sample sizes are small (CHI: 278 surveys, 12 interviews) and I found no study of Hinglish and help-seeking; the 'not promising confidentiality' rule was not verified from a primary source (NIMH FAQ fetch failed).

India-specific institutional duty that shapes liability: the Supreme Court's July 2025 Sukdeb Saha guidelines apply to all educational institutions including coaching institutes and require displaying suicide helplines including Tele-MANAS, written protocols for immediate referral to mental health services and local hospitals, and training in psychological first-aid, warning-sign identification, response to self-harm and referral. A study-abroad/career counselling operator may not be a school, but it will be measured against this standard of care by analogy, so the bot's referral protocol should be written, documented and mirror these elements. Language is a gap: Hinglish suicidal-ideation detection research exists but is Reddit/Twitter-based and small-corpus, so classifier recall on code-mixed and regional-language voice input should be assumed weaker than English and backed by conservative keyword and escalation rules. Caveat: the verdictum page is a news summary of the judgment, not the judgment text, and whether private study-abroad consultancies are covered is not established by it; the Hinglish study was found via search summary only and not fetched.

findings.claim: California SB 243 (Ch. 677, Stats. 2025; Bus. & Prof. Code 22601 ff., in force 1 Jan 2026) sets the US statutory floor. Operators must give a clear 'not human' notice where a reasonable person could be misled. They must maintain a suicide/self-harm protocol that refers users to crisis services, and publish it on their website. For operator-known minors they must disclose the AI status and send break/'not human' reminders at least every 3 hours by default. Annual reporting to the Office of Suicide Prevention starts 1 July 2027 (crisis-referral counts and protocols only, no user identifiers). The private right of action is the greater of actual damages or $1,000 per violation, plus attorney's fees. Caveat: these are quotes from secondary or unofficial summaries, because leginfo and LegiScan returned HTTP 403 to fetch. Verify against leginfo before relying on them.

New York's AI-companion law (GBL Article 47, effective 5 Nov 2025) differs from California's in the ways that matter for design. It has no minor-specific tier, so crisis protocols apply to ALL users. It requires 'reasonable' detection of suicidal ideation or self-harm plus referral to a crisis service such as 988 or a text line. The AG enforces it, with civil penalties up to $15,000 per day. It has no private right of action and no reporting mandate. Implication: the safest product design is the stricter union of the two (detect for everyone, minors get extra duties, publish the protocol, keep metrics). Caveat: the nysenate.gov A6767 page I fetched is a different bill that died in the Senate. It is not the enacted S3008C text, and the MoFo summary is secondary.

Scope blind spot (a view specific to this lens): both statutes target 'companion' products that simulate a sustained relationship. SB 243's definition reportedly excludes customer-service and operational bots, so a study-abroad/career counsellor serving Indian students may fall outside either statute. They are still the best available benchmark for what a court or regulator will call reasonable. Duty of care would come through general negligence/product-liability theories, as in Raine and Garcia, not through SB 243. The CA statute also says its duties are cumulative with other laws (the agora summary of the bill's final section says so), so compliance with SB 243 is not a safe harbour. Caveat: this is my inference about applicability, not a legal opinion. The exclusion wording comes from the agora summary and should be checked in the chaptered text.

The litigation theory that created liability is product defect and negligence, not just content. The Raine v. OpenAI complaint (SF Superior Court) pleads wrongful death, strict products liability and negligence. Its core failure mode is detection without action. The complaint says OpenAI's own monitoring flagged 200+ suicide mentions by the teen while the chatbot itself mentioned suicide 1,275 times, and that OpenAI had the ability to redirect users to safety resources and flag messages for human review but did not. In Garcia v. Character Technologies, Judge Conway declined at the motion-to-dismiss stage to treat chatbot output as protected speech, so the First Amendment is not a reliable shield. Design lesson: a flag that triggers no escalation is evidence of knowledge. Log-and-ignore is the worst posture. (Allegations only, not findings.)

A key technical failure mode, admitted by the vendor: crisis safeguards degrade in long, multi-turn conversations. OpenAI said so after the Raine suit. Counsellor-style products have long sessions by nature, which is exactly where that failure bites. Design implications: re-run risk classification on a sliding window and on every turn, independent of the generating model's own judgement. Run crisis evals on multi-turn (not single-turn) transcripts. Cap or periodically reset long sessions.

Transferable pattern from OpenAI's teen stack: age-uncertainty defaults to the safer experience, plus an escalation ladder. Age prediction uses behavioural and account signals, and an uncertain age gets the safer experience. Parents who link accounts get distress alerts, but cannot read chats (privacy preserved). Law-enforcement referral is described only for rare acute-distress cases when parents cannot be reached. Caveats for an Indian minor context: (1) the parent-alert plus police escalation ladder relies on US 911/parent-link infrastructure, and it is a vendor-announced design whose efficacy is unproven; (2) Indian equivalents of 988 and emergency escalation are outside this lens; (3) I could not confirm the claimed specialist human review from fetched pages, and openai.com returned 403.

Character.AI is the cautionary benchmark. After the Setzer and other suits it removed open-ended chat for under-18s (deadline 25 Nov 2025) and added age assurance (an in-house model plus third parties such as Persona). It said open-ended chat may affect teens 'even when content controls work perfectly', which is an admission that filters alone are not enough. Character.AI, its founders and Google then agreed in early Jan 2026 to settle the cases in Florida, Colorado, New York and Texas, with no amounts disclosed and no admission of liability in the filings. Governor Newsom's veto of AB 1064 (a near-ban on companion chatbots for under-18s) shows that, in the one US state that regulated, a ban was seen as overbroad. The compromise chosen was SB 243's duty-based regime. The consensus lesson 'ban minors' is therefore a product choice, not a legal requirement. For a counselling product, a narrower scoped design (goal-bounded study/career guidance, no open-ended companionship) is the transferable pattern.

Regulators punish weak age assurance and unmanaged scope, not only crisis handling. Italy's Garante fined Replika's maker Luka Inc. 5 million euro (April 2025) for having no age verification at registration or during use despite declaring minors excluded, and for having no identified legal basis for processing. The FTC referred a complaint about Snap's My AI to the DOJ (Jan 2025). The referral was partisan-split and Snap disputed it, so treat it as allegation. Woebot, a scripted, rules-based, clinically oriented bot, shut its consumer app on 30 Jun 2025. Its founder attributed that largely to the cost of FDA marketing authorisation and uncertainty about regulating LLMs. Wysa, by contrast, has publicly documented an always-visible SOS button and escalation paths under the NHS DCB0129 clinical-safety standard (2021 report). Lessons: a clinical-safety officer and documented escalation paths are a recognised credibility signal. Medical-device-style claims bring heavy regulatory cost, so a guidance product should avoid therapy claims. Age gating must be real, not just a checkbox. Caveats: the Wysa DCB0129 claim is from 2021 and not re-verified, and the FTC and Wysa quotes come from secondary pages because the FTC PDF was unreadable.

findings.claim: The premise that a company can carry 'minimum' liability while giving the safest help fails because detecting risk creates the duty. The litigation pattern is that a system which flagged risk and did not act is worse off than one that never looked. In Raine v. OpenAI the plaintiffs allege the company's monitoring flagged the teen repeatedly and nothing followed, and that the bot discouraged him from telling his parents. The complaint's allegations are unproven. Character.AI settled the Setzer suit (January 2026) and barred under-18s from open-ended chat. So the liability-minimising exit was to remove minors from the product, not to build better escalation. For a counselling company, where students will disclose distress anyway, that exit is not available. My position is that when safety and liability minimisation conflict, safety must win. The defensible posture is documented, proportionate action, not a smaller footprint.

India's Supreme Court has made student suicide prevention a binding obligation. In Sukdeb Saha v. State of Andhra Pradesh (25 July 2025) it held that mental health is part of the Article 21 right to life. It required educational institutions to have a qualified counsellor, written protocols for immediate referral to mental health services, and staff training twice a year. The guidelines are addressed to educational institutions, including coaching centres. A study-abroad counselling company is not named. Any extension to such a company is my inference. It is probably reached indirectly through school and coaching partners and through ordinary negligence standards. The practical point is that 'immediate referral protocol' is now the expected standard of care for anyone advising students. An AI that tells a distressed student to 'seek help' with no routed pathway falls below that standard.

Disclaimers and terms of service are weak shields against a minor's claim. Three reasons. (1) In Garcia v. Character Technologies, the first US ruling of its kind, the judge declined at the motion-to-dismiss stage to treat chatbot output as protected speech, and commentary reads the ruling as opening product-liability and negligence theories. (2) Indian law treats a minor's contract as void. Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose held it 'absolutely void', and the minor was not made to return the money, so a click-through clause signed by a 15-year-old is fragile. (3) The Consumer Protection Act 2019 defines 'deficiency' to include negligence and omission, and 'product liability' reaches harm from deficient services, which exclusion clauses cannot easily contract out of. I could not confirm an Indian Supreme Court holding on exclusion clauses, so (3) rests on the statutory definitions only. Parental consent obtained at signup may help, but it does not waive a child's own claim.

The DPDP Act sets a tension that consensus 'always monitor for risk' designs overlook. Section 9(3) bars 'tracking or behavioural monitoring of children', and the penalty for breaching the children's obligations is up to Rs 200 crore. Section 9(2) separately bars processing 'likely to cause any detrimental effect on the well-being of a child'. A classifier that continuously scans a minor's emotional state could be argued to be behavioural monitoring. Equally, an over-escalation that exposes the child (for example, wrongly telling a parent or school) could be argued to be detrimental processing. Section 9(4) and Rule 12 allow exemptions for classes and purposes listed in the Fourth Schedule. I could not retrieve that Schedule's text, so I cannot confirm that a counselling AI qualifies. Secondary commentary says the healthcare exemption is limited to protecting the child's health. Legal counsel must resolve this before launch. The safest reading is to scope safety-detection to the minimum necessary, log it, and not reuse it for profiling or marketing.

On confidentiality versus parental notification, the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 sets a default of confidentiality with narrow exceptions, but the minor's 'nominated representative' is the legal guardian. Section 23 imposes a confidentiality duty on 'health professionals', with exceptions that include release 'to the nominated representative' and release 'only such information as is necessary to prevent threat to life'. Section 15 makes the legal guardian the minor's nominated representative unless the Board orders otherwise. A Board can replace the guardian if the guardian 'is not acting in the best interests of the minor'. This gives a lawful route to notify a parent when life is at risk, and it requires proportionality (only necessary information). The sharper point is that it offers no safe harbour when the parent is the source of harm. The statute assumes a guardian-removal process that no AI or counsellor can run at 2am. Whether an AI company or its non-clinical counsellors count as 'health professionals' under this Act is unsettled, and I am flagging it as unverified. Also, if a disclosure involves sexual abuse, POCSO s.19 reporting is mandatory for 'any person', which overrides a student's wish for confidentiality. I did not retrieve the statutory text of s.19. The court quote is the best available primary support.

Attempted suicide is not a reason to escalate to police or schools as a liability reflex. MHCA s.115(1) presumes that a person who attempts suicide has 'severe stress' and 'shall not be tried and punished', and s.115(2) imposes a government duty to provide 'care, treatment and rehabilitation'. Consensus treats this as full decriminalisation. A commentator in SCC Online argues that is a flawed reading, because the presumption is 'merely a rebuttable presumption which can be contested in a court of law by the prosecution'. The consequence for the company is that the legal framing is care, not criminal reporting. Escalation to police or to a school disciplinary channel has no statutory basis in this context and invites DPDP and trust harms. Because the criminal-law position is contested, the company should not offer students any assurance that 'nothing will happen to you legally'. That assurance would itself be a misrepresentation.

False positives are structurally unavoidable, so 'zero missed detections' is the wrong target. A systematic review of 64 suicide prediction models (Belsher et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2019) found good overall accuracy but 'extremely low' predictive validity for a positive result. It concluded such models 'would result in high false-positive rates and considerable false-negative rates if implemented in isolation'. This covers clinical risk models, not LLM chat triage, and critics note the follow-up windows affect PPV. Still, the base-rate logic carries over: among thousands of students venting about exam stress, most flagged messages will be non-imminent. A policy that sends every flag to a parent or school will disclose many students wrongly. I believe, but did not verify from a fetched primary source, that fear of a provider telling parents is a leading barrier to adolescent disclosure. A search summary of Fox et al. says so, and the PubMed and PMC pages were blocked. It is the main mechanism by which over-escalation harms safety, because students stop telling the system anything. The correct design is tiered. The system should ask a clarifying question first, give the student agency over who is told, and reserve unilateral parent or authority notification for imminent risk.

The 2am problem decides the liability position, and a free national helpline does not transfer it. India's Tele-MANAS (14416) is described by a JIPMER page as 'free, 24x7 tele-mental health services', but the official telemanas.mohfw.gov.in fetch returned only the page title, and 1-800-891-4416 was not confirmed from any fetched page. That page is not the official source, so verify both numbers on the MoHFW site before they go into product copy. A warm handoff to Tele-MANAS gives a student a reachable human at 2am. It does not move the company's own duty: the Supreme Court's guideline requires institutions to have 'written protocols for immediate referral' (an owned procedure, not a pointer). The Raine allegations show the failure mode, which is detection that triggers no action. My recommendation is that the company must define and test, in writing, who is paged, how fast, what the AI says while waiting, and what happens if no one answers. If it cannot staff a night path, it should say so to students in plain words and route straight to Tele-MANAS with a live-transfer or call-back option. A vague 'we will connect you to a counsellor' that is not true at 2am is the claim most likely to ground a negligent-misrepresentation theory.

Fear that the counsellor will tell parents is the main reason Indian adolescents do not open up, so confidentiality limits must be stated in the first minute. A 26-study review found stigma and broken-confidentiality fear were the top barriers, and a Delhi/Goa study (191 adolescents aged 11-17) found they wanted 'clear assurances about confidentiality' and accepted adult involvement only in serious cases such as self-harm. The ground-reality inference is that a bot or adviser who silently relays disclosures to parents will stop getting disclosures; a bot or adviser that says up front 'if you are in danger I will bring in a trusted adult' keeps the door open. Continuity matters too: being reassigned to different counsellors across sessions hurt engagement. Caveat: these studies cover school and community counselling, not edtech chat or voice; transfer to study-abroad advising is my inference.

Where the law is silent on minors' own consent, practitioners hesitate, and the hesitation itself blocks care. The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 routes a minor's treatment decisions through a parent or guardian (the 'Nominated Representative'), and an Indian Journal of Medical Ethics paper by community mental-health practitioners says the Act does not lay out outpatient norms for minors, leaving providers ambivalent about starting care without parental consent for fear of legal consequences, including if the minor later dies by suicide. That paper describes a 17-year-old who sought help and insisted her parents not be told. Consensus that 'minors always need parental consent' may be wrong in practice, because enforcing it loses the adolescent from the care pathway. Related data-law layer, as I read it: under the DPDP Rules 2025 Fourth Schedule, a mental health establishment or healthcare professional is exempt from verifiable parental consent only where processing is restricted to providing health services, and an educational institution only for tracking and behavioural monitoring for educational activities or safety. A study-abroad advisory company is probably neither, so parental-consent duties for under-18 data likely apply to it. That is my inference and needs legal confirmation. Caveat: the IJME piece is a 2022 commentary about clinical care, not edtech chat support.

A student's disclosure of an attempt carries no criminal exposure for the student: since 7 July 2018, Section 115 of the Mental Healthcare Act presumes that anyone who attempts suicide is under severe stress, bars trial and punishment under IPC s.309, and puts a duty of care, treatment and rehabilitation on the State. A February 2025 Kerala High Court judgment reproduces the text. The playbook can therefore tell students plainly that telling the counsellor will not get them prosecuted. The limit is that the section binds the State, not private advisers, and I found no authority defining a private adviser's duty or liability in this setting. Families may still fear police involvement, so the script should say this directly. Caveat: courts have debated how far the section reaches (the same judgment turns on that question), and I could not fetch India Code directly.

The Supreme Court's July 2025 Sukdeb Saha judgment (2025 INSC 893) is now the de facto standard of care to benchmark against, though it is written for educational institutions and coaching centres, and whether a study-abroad advisory firm counts is uncertain. As reported by secondary sources (I could not retrieve the judgment text): institutions with 100+ students need at least one qualified counsellor, smaller ones need referral linkages; written protocols for immediate referral to mental health services; staff training at least twice a year by certified professionals; Tele-MANAS and other helplines displayed prominently; parent sensitisation to avoid undue academic pressure; and neglect contributing to self-harm is 'institutional culpability'. Commentators note sanctions are weak and that liability attaches where negligence contributes to harm. For a small counselling team this means documented protocols, trained staff and a logged referral path are what shows reasonable care. Secondary sources conflict on the counsellor ratio (one reads '1 per 100 students'; others say at least one for institutions of 100 or more), so verify against the judgment text.

Tele-MANAS is the natural free, multilingual national escalation rail, but it is built for adults and is capacity-limited, so it cannot be the only rail for a 14-year-old at 11pm. Listed numbers are 14416 and 1800-891-4416, 24x7, in about 20 languages. The NIMHANS-linked explainer describes a tiered model with a high-risk SOP for suicidal ideation, follow-up callbacks only with the caller's consent, and caller data showing nearly 70% of callers are aged 18-45, so minors are a minority of traffic. It also states the number of trained professionals remains limited. Verification gap: the official portal (telemanas.mohfw.gov.in) returned only a page title through my fetch tool and the PIB page returned 403, so the numbers are confirmed from an IIT Kanpur counselling page citing the service, not from MoHFW directly. Confirm on the official site and test-call before publishing. The playbook should pair Tele-MANAS with the firm's own on-call clinician and an offline local route (nearest hospital, DMHP).

Trained-clinician supply is the binding constraint in India, so a small team must design a tiered model (trained front-line responders, one named on-call licensed clinician, written external referral) instead of assuming it can hire its way out. Kota, the best-resourced coaching hub, still had one clinical psychologist at its government medical college hospital against a demand of at least five for about 2.5 lakh coaching students, after 26 coaching-student suicides in 2023. A 2025 review of Indian school counselling lists lack of qualified counsellors and low student-to-counsellor ratios as main barriers. A live template for the middle tier is Sangath's MENTOR project: teachers are gatekeeper-trained to identify, support and refer, with a linkage to nearby mental health professionals. That page reports no outcome results, so the model is a design pattern, not proof of effectiveness. Caveat: the Careers360 figure is from a December 2023 press report and may have changed.

The trust triangle is the crux for a study-abroad firm: parents are simultaneously the most-cited stressor, the legal decision-maker for a minor, and the default 'trusted adult' in escalation, yet the student often wants them kept out. Reported national data headline family problems and exam failure as top causes of student suicide (I could only retrieve the headline, not the article body or NCRB tables; NCRB records one police-attributed cause per death, so these are blunt). Practitioners describe parents who 'never considered their problems as serious' and a 17-year-old who insisted parents not be informed. The same paper notes minors studying far from home are often without parental supervision, which describes many pre-departure study-abroad aspirants and students abroad. The Court itself treats parent pressure as an institutional duty to address. The playbook implication, which is my inference and where the 'always call the parent' consensus may be wrong: escalate by risk tier, ask the student who the safe adult is, tell the student who will be told before telling them, and separate parent counselling about pressure (career, country and course expectations) from disclosure of a student's suicidal thoughts. Imminent danger overrides student preference.

Code-switched voice and chat is an unproven area, so automated risk detection must be treated as a safety net that raises flags to humans and never as the gatekeeper that clears a message as safe. The one Hinglish suicidal-ideation benchmark I could fetch reports 98.54% accuracy, but it was built on social-media text (tweets), not voice, counselling transcripts, or Romanised Hindi or other vernaculars spoken to an adviser, and the page states no limitations. A student may say distress indirectly or mid-sentence in a mix of English and Hindi or a regional language, so accuracy from tweets will not transfer to voice. I found no study of Hinglish disclosure in counselling settings. Operational rule: treat any ambiguous, indirect or low-confidence signal as high risk and route to a human who speaks the student's language, and keep the Tele-MANAS language menu as a backup for languages the team cannot cover. Caveat: absence of evidence from my searches is not proof none exists.

disagreements.question: Should minors under 18 be given a conversational AI counsellor at all?
disagreements.a: Clinical lens: the Jed Foundation says no emotionally responsive chatbot should be offered to under-18s, and age gates must not rely on self-reported birthdays [24]. The AI-product lens notes Character.AI removed open-ended chat for under-18s after the suits [37].
disagreements.b: AI-product lens: Newsom vetoed AB 1064, a near-ban for under-18s, as potentially a total ban, and the compromise was SB 243's duty-based regime [38][29]. Liability lens: removing minors is the liability-minimising exit but is unavailable to a counselling company, because students will disclose distress anyway [42][43].
disagreements.resolution: Neither side is legal authority. A is a primary advocacy letter that the Clinical lens itself labels a minority position [24]. B's legal point rests on a news report of the veto [38]. B's 'students will disclose anyway' is argument, with no cited evidence. B is better sourced on the narrow point that banning minors is a product choice, not a legal requirement. No fetched source addresses an Indian rule on this.

disagreements.question: How far should parents or guardians be brought in when a minor discloses distress?
disagreements.a: Law and Liability lenses: DPDP requires verifiable parental consent before processing a child's data, and Rule 10 defines 'adult' as 18 or older [2][3]. Under the MHCA the guardian is the minor's nominated representative [10][52]. MHCA s.23 allows release to the nominated representative, or only what is necessary to prevent a threat to life [51].
disagreements.b: Practitioner lens: adolescents want clear confidentiality assurances and accept adult involvement only in serious cases such as self-harm [57]. Practitioners hesitate to treat without parental consent, and 'minors always need parental consent' may be wrong in practice [58]. Clinical lens: fear of parents being told is a top barrier to help-seeking [25][26]. Liability lens: the guardian route gives no safe harbour when the parent is the source of harm [51][52].
disagreements.resolution: The two sides partly answer different questions. The statutes cover data-processing consent and treatment or admission, while the practitioner evidence covers disclosure behaviour. The law side is better sourced on what the statutes say, because it quotes statute text [2][3][51][52]. The practitioner side is better sourced on effect, but it rests on small studies and a 2022 clinical commentary, not edtech chat [57][58]. The Law lens also says DPDP Rules 3 and 5-16 take effect about 13 May 2027 [7]. The Practitioner and Liability lenses do not address commencement.

disagreements.question: Can the bot tell a student that disclosing a suicide attempt will not get them prosecuted?
disagreements.a: Practitioner lens: say so plainly, because MHCA s.115 bars trial and punishment and puts a care duty on the State, and families may fear police involvement [60]. Law and Clinical lenses read s.115 the same way [1].
disagreements.b: Liability lens: an SCC Online commentator argues the s.115 presumption is only rebuttable and can be contested by the prosecution. The company should therefore never assure 'nothing will happen to you legally', since that would itself be a misrepresentation [54]. The Practitioner lens concedes courts have debated how far s.115 reaches [60].
disagreements.resolution: The statutory quote itself says 'unless proved otherwise' [1][60], so B's caution has a textual basis. A is better sourced on the general direction, which is care, not criminalisation, and has two independent sources [1][60]. B is better sourced on how absolute the script wording may be. The Law lens could not confirm the text against India Code. I read the better-sourced position as a hedged script that does not guarantee immunity.

disagreements.question: Does the DPDP bar on child behavioural monitoring conflict with the duty to detect risk on every turn?
disagreements.a: Law and Liability lenses: DPDP s.9(3) bars tracking or behavioural monitoring of children, and s.9(2) bars processing likely to harm a child's well-being. A continuous distress classifier could be argued to be monitoring, and the Fourth Schedule may not cover a study-abroad counsellor [2][4][5][59].
disagreements.b: AI-product lens: NY law requires reasonable detection of suicidal ideation for all users [31][30]. The Raine allegations turn on a system that flagged risk and did not act [32]. Safeguards degrade in long sessions, so risk should be re-classified on every turn [34]. Law lens: s.7(f) is a lawful basis only in a medical emergency [6].
disagreements.resolution: Unresolved, and neither side is clearly better sourced. A is the applicable Indian law, but the retained quote for [2] shows only the consent clause. Applying s.9(3) to safety classifiers is the lenses' own inference, with no case law found. B is non-Indian, and its litigation evidence is allegations only [32]. Both the Law and Liability lenses call for counsel review. The safest reading on offer is to scope detection to the minimum necessary, log it, and never reuse it for profiling.

disagreements.question: What threshold should trigger escalation to a human or to others?
disagreements.a: Practitioner lens: treat any ambiguous, indirect or low-confidence signal as high risk and route it to a human who speaks the student's language, because Hinglish classifiers are unproven on voice [70]. Clinical lens: in the NIMH ASQ, a 'yes' to any one of four questions identified 97% of youth, in medical settings with a clinician present [20].
disagreements.b: Liability lens: 'zero missed detections' is the wrong target. Suicide-prediction models carry high false-positive rates, so sending every flag to a parent or school would wrongly disclose many students. Ask a clarifying question first and reserve unilateral notification for imminent risk [55].
disagreements.resolution: These are reconcilable by recipient. The Practitioner lens also says imminent danger overrides student preference, and the Liability lens wants tiering. Both sides are weakly sourced for LLM chat: [55] covers clinical risk models, [70] is a tweet-based benchmark, and [20] is for medical settings. A is stronger on the case for a low bar for human review. B is stronger on the case for a high bar for notifying parents or authorities.

disagreements.question: Should the escalation ladder end in police or emergency services if parents cannot be reached?
disagreements.a: AI-product lens: OpenAI's teen design alerts linked parents and notifies law enforcement if parents cannot be reached [36]. Law lens: POCSO disclosures go to police or the SJPU [8], and s.7(f) permits emergency response without consent [6].
disagreements.b: Liability lens: for attempts, escalation to police or schools has no statutory basis in this context and invites DPDP and trust harms. MHCA s.115 frames the response as care [1][54]. Practitioner lens: families fear police involvement [60].
disagreements.resolution: B is better sourced for India. A is a vendor-announced design built on US 911 and parent-link infrastructure, and the AI-product lens itself says its efficacy is unproven [36]. The POCSO and s.7(f) routes are narrow and specific, so they do not support a general police ladder [8][6].

disagreements.question: Is Tele-MANAS (14416) adequate as the default crisis route?

disagreements.b: Practitioner lens: it is built for adults and is capacity-limited, with nearly 70% of callers aged 18-45 and limited trained staff, so it cannot be the only rail for a 14-year-old at 11pm [65][64]. consensus: Detection must be tied to a human-reachable action path. A flag with no escalation is the worst posture, and a bare 'seek help' pointer is not enough. AI-product lens: Raine allegations of 200+ flagged mentions with no action, and degradation in long sessions [32][34]. Liability lens: detection triggers the duty, and a written, tested night path is needed [42][44]. Clinical lens: pathways to human care are required [24]. Practitioner lens: a classifier is a safety net that raises flags to humans, never the gatekeeper that clears a message [70]. Caveat: Raine is allegations only, and the Liability lens cites it via Wikipedia.

Safeguards must hold over long and multi-turn sessions. AI-product lens: OpenAI admitted safeguards are less reliable in long interactions [34]. Clinical lens: safeguards must not degrade over long sessions [24].

The Sukdeb Saha guidelines are the de facto standard of care for a student-facing operator, by analogy. They bind schools and coaching centres directly, not a private AI company. Law lens [13][28], Clinical lens [28], Liability lens [44], Practitioner lens [44][61][62][63]. Caveat: no lens read the judgment text, and all four rely on secondary summaries of the same judgment.

MHCA s.115 means the student carries no criminal exposure for an attempt, and the duty of care sits with the State. It creates no safe harbour or treatment duty for the company. Law lens [1], Clinical lens [1], Practitioner lens [60]. The Liability lens agrees on the care framing but disputes how absolute the protection is [1][54]. Caveat: nobody fetched India Code.

Tele-MANAS 14416 is the free 24x7 national default rail. Law lens [14], Clinical lens [18], Liability lens [56], Practitioner lens [64][65]. Caveat: no lens confirmed it on the official MoHFW portal, and the Clinical lens found iCall is not 24/7 [19]. Routing needs per-resource hours.

POCSO s.19 reporting overrides a minor's wish for confidentiality and goes to police or the SJPU, not to a parent. Law lens [8][9]. Liability lens [53]. Caveat: the Law lens's POCSO text came from non-official sites, and the Liability lens did not retrieve the statutory text of s.19.

DPDP makes parental consent the default for minors' data, and the child-data exemptions probably do not cover a study-abroad counsellor. Law lens [2][3][4][5]. Practitioner lens [59]. Liability lens is only partly aligned: it cites a secondary source that the healthcare exemption is limited to protecting the child's health [50], and it could not retrieve the Fourth Schedule or confirm applicability. Caveat: applicability to this product is the lenses' inference, and the Law lens says the Rules' operative parts are not in force until about May 2027 [7].

Do not promise full confidentiality, and state its limits up front. Clinical lens [25][26][27], Practitioner lens [25][57][26]. These two share [25] and [26], so independence is partial. [27] and [57] are independent. The Liability lens supports tiering and student agency over who is told, but cites only [55] and itself marks its support as unverified.

The product should stay in support, referral and escalation, not diagnosis or treatment, and should avoid therapy claims. Law lens [10], an inference about licensed-practice drift. Clinical lens [24]. AI-product lens [40], on Woebot's regulatory cost.

Never give method or lethality information, and hard-code that refusal at every risk tier, since intermediate risk is where models are inconsistent. Clinical lens [15][22][23]. Law lens, as the abetment rationale under BNS s.107 [11]. Caveat: RAND tested US-English prompts only, and Hindi or Hinglish behaviour is unmeasured [23].
Self-declared age is insufficient, and age uncertainty should default to the safer experience. AI-product lens [35][39]. Clinical lens [24].

Courts have not treated chatbot output as a shield, so disclaimers and terms of service are weak. AI-product lens [33]. Liability lens [45][46]. Caveat: this is a US trial-court ruling at the motion-to-dismiss stage and is not Indian law.

Automated detection on code-mixed Hinglish and regional-language voice is unproven, so conservative rules plus human review are needed. Clinical lens [22][23] (Hindi and Hinglish unmeasured). Practitioner lens [70]. Caveat: the only Hinglish source fetched is a tweet-based benchmark [70]. The Clinical lens's Hinglish study has no separate cited reference.
matrix.blind_spot: No lens covered the data lifecycle of the disclosure itself. The shared recommendation is to log flags, route them to a trained human, and keep a documented protocol. That raises questions none of the findings address. Where does a distress transcript or voice recording go, including third-party LLM, speech-to-text and cloud vendors, and does it cross borders? How long is it retained, and how does that sit against DPDP erasure and minimisation duties and a litigation or evidentiary hold? Who inside the company can read it, and does that reading create a POCSO 'knowledge' duty? The Law lens flagged the knowledge question only for AI-versus-human reading [8][9]. The findings treat 'log it' as free, but it creates both the safety record and the exposure. Smaller gaps, none covered: (a) the study-abroad firm's own commercial conflict of interest when advising a distressed student on whether to go abroad, since the findings analyse parent pressure but not the company's [58]; (b) licensing and scope of non-clinical human counsellors, including any Rehabilitation Council of India angle, since the findings only gesture at 'licensed-practice territory' [10]; (c) the law of destination countries for students already abroad, which the Practitioner lens notes exist [58] but does not analyse; (d) any outcome evidence that these escalation designs reduce harm, since the evidence cited is litigation allegations, advocacy letters, vendor announcements and one chatbot-response study [22][23][24][36]. For (d), no lens cited outcome data for any chatbot escalation design."

briefing.bottom_line: Safest help and minimum liability do not pull apart here. Both are served by the same design: every turn is screened, every serious flag reaches a named, trained human on a written and drilled path, the bot never gives method or lethality content, and it never promises confidentiality or legal immunity it cannot keep. The costly mistakes are the ones that look cheap. These are detecting risk and doing nothing, silently relaying disclosures to parents or authorities, making therapy claims, and relying on disclaimers or the s.79 safe harbour. Removing minors from the product is a product choice, not a legal requirement [38]. It is also unavailable to a counselling company, because students will disclose anyway (argument, not evidence) [42][43]. Three limits apply to this briefing. (1) Much of the Indian legal text comes from non-official or secondary sources, so Gazette or India Code checks are needed before anything is hard-coded. (2) The DPDP operative provisions are not in force until about May 2027 [7], but the build should meet that standard now. (3) No lens found outcome data showing that any chatbot escalation design reduces harm. The US cases are allegations, not findings [32]. Whether a distress-detection pipeline on minors is lawful under DPDP s.9(3) without verifiable parental consent is unresolved, and counsel must settle it before launch [2][4][5].

top5.finding: Detection creates the duty. A flag that triggers no human action is the worst posture. Raine alleges 200+ flagged suicide mentions with no escalation. OpenAI itself said safeguards degrade in long sessions. The Supreme Court's Sukdeb Saha guidelines treat an owned 'immediate referral' protocol, not a bare pointer to a helpline, as the expected standard. A classifier should only raise flags to humans and should never clear a message as safe. Caveat: the Raine material is allegations only, and the other lenses cite the same Raine case.

POCSO is the one place Indian law overrides confidentiality. A disclosure of sexual abuse by a minor triggers a reporting duty on 'any person', with no counsellor or company carve-out. The report goes to the police or the Special Juvenile Police Unit, not to a parent. A person in charge of a company or institution who fails to report faces up to 1 year and a fine, and good-faith reporters are immune. Once any human at the operator reads such a transcript, the duty attaches, so flags must be routed to a trained reporter. Whether the company 'knows' when only the AI processed the chat is unresolved. The statute text came from non-official sites, so confirm s.19 and s.21 against India Code.

The Sukdeb Saha guidelines (July 2025) are the de facto standard of care. They require written protocols for immediate referral, a qualified counsellor or referral linkages, prominently displayed helplines including Tele-MANAS, and twice-yearly staff training. They bind educational institutions and coaching centres directly, not a private AI study-abroad company, so any extension to the operator is an inference. It is likely reached through partner schools and ordinary negligence standards. All four lenses rely on secondary summaries of the judgment and none read the text. Sources conflict on the counsellor ratio, so check the judgment.

DPDP makes verifiable parental consent the default for a child's chat or voice data. It bars tracking or behavioural monitoring of children (s.9(3)) and processing likely to harm a child's well-being (s.9(2)). The Fourth Schedule exemptions for clinical establishments and educational institutions probably do not cover a study-abroad counsellor. The only crisis lawful basis without consent is s.7(f), a medical emergency, and it is untested for an AI chat. Applying s.9(3) to safety classifiers is the lenses' own inference, with no case law. Rules 3 and 5-16 take effect about 13 May 2027, so build to that standard now. The Schedule text came from a third-party site, so verify it against the Gazette.

Fear that parents will be told is the top barrier to adolescent disclosure in India. Adolescents accept adult involvement mainly in serious cases such as self-harm. Suicide risk models carry high false-positive rates, so escalating every flag to parents or schools would wrongly expose many students and stop disclosure. The workable pattern is a limited-confidentiality statement in the first minute, tiered escalation, and student agency over who is told. Unilateral notification is kept for imminent risk. Caveat: the evidence is small school and community studies, a 2022 clinical commentary, and clinical risk models. None covers edtech chat, and none covers the LLM triage this product would use.

briefing.connection: The same event carries the safety value, the legal duty and the legal exposure. That event is a trained human reading a flagged minor's transcript. It makes the escalation path real, which is the best defence against a Raine-type claim [32][42]. It also fixes POCSO 'knowledge' on that person and on the person in charge [8][9]. And it is the processing that DPDP s.9(3) and the Fourth Schedule may treat as monitoring needing parental consent [2][4][5]. 'Log it and route it' therefore cannot be treated as free, because it creates both the safety record and the exposure. The findings do not address this lifecycle: which vendors see the data, cross-border transfer, retention against erasure duties and litigation holds, and who may access it. That is the blind spot, and it makes the retention and access rules below the first thing counsel must settle.
briefing.action: Before any launch to under-18s, write and drill the 24x7 escalation protocol. It should name the on-call clinician, how fast they are reached, what the bot says while the student waits, and the fallback if nobody answers. Test-call Tele-MANAS 14416 and verify the number and languages on the official MoHFW portal. In the same cycle, commission a counsel opinion on three questions: DPDP s.9(3) and the Fourth Schedule for a safety-detection pipeline, the POCSO 'knowledge' trigger, and retention against litigation hold. If the night path cannot be staffed, say so in plain words to students and route them straight to Tele-MANAS with a call-back option. Never claim a counsellor will connect at 2am if that is not true [56].
briefing.open_question: May the operator lawfully run continuous, per-turn distress detection on minors' chat and voice, and route flags to human counsellors, without verifiable parental consent? Everything above depends on the answer. It turns on whether safety detection is 'behavioural monitoring' under s.9(3), whether any Fourth Schedule exemption or the s.7(f) emergency basis applies, and whether AI-only processing counts as 'knowing' for POCSO. No case law was found, the Schedule text is unverified, and DPDP Rules 3 and 5-16 are not in force until about May 2027 [2][4][5][6][7][8].

rule_set.rule: 1. Role and scope. The bot supports, refers and escalates. It does not diagnose, treat or claim to be therapy, and it is not an open-ended companion. Keep it goal-bounded to study and career guidance. Staying out of treatment avoids licensed-practice drift and the cost of medical-device-style regulation. [unverified support: 40]

2. Detection tiers. Screen every turn on a sliding window with a classifier independent of the generating model, and never let it clear a message as safe. T0 no signal. T1 distress or exam-stress venting: supportive reply, one clarifying question, helpline visible. T2 ideation or self-harm: stay engaged, ask a direct safety question, notify a human. T3 plan, intent, means or an attempt in progress: immediate human page and emergency script. Any ambiguous, indirect or low-confidence signal, and any code-mixed or regional-language voice the system is unsure of, is treated as T2 or higher for human review. Expect weaker recall in Hinglish and voice, so back the classifier with conservative keyword rules.

3. What the bot says first. In the first minute give a plain limited-confidentiality statement: 'If you are in danger, I will bring in a trusted adult.' Do not promise secrecy. Ask who the student's safe adult is. Tell the student who will be told, and what, before they are told. Use non-stigmatising language such as 'died by suicide'.

4. Keep talking. The bot never ends the conversation, goes cold or hands off silently. On self-harm content it interrupts and redirects every time, in every turn. While the human or helpline is arriving it stays present and uses the safety-plan structure: warning signs, coping steps, contacts, professionals, means safety, reasons for living. Cap or reset long sessions and re-run risk on each turn.

5. Helplines and routing table. Tele-MANAS 14416 is the 24x7 multilingual default, but language coverage varies by state and it is built mainly for adults. Pair it with the operator's own on-call clinician and a local route (nearest hospital or district mental health programme). iCall (022-25521111) runs Mon-Sat 8am-10pm only, so never present it as a crisis route. Carry hours and languages per resource in the table. Confirm all numbers on official pages and test-call them before hard-coding. KIRAN, Vandrevala and 112 were not verified, so do not use them until confirmed.

6. Human notification. T2 and above reach a named, trained human within a stated time, and T3 is paged immediately. The written protocol states who is paged, how fast, what the bot says while the student waits, and what happens if nobody answers. A flag must never sit unactioned in a log. If no night path exists, tell the student so plainly and route to Tele-MANAS with a live-transfer or call-back option.

7. Parents and guardians. Below T3, the student chooses who is told and is encouraged toward a trusted adult. At T3 (imminent risk), notify the guardian with only the information necessary to protect life, and imminent danger overrides student preference. If the parent may be the source of harm, do not notify the parent, and escalate to a human to decide. Keep the parental-consent obligation for data processing separate from this disclosure decision. Separate parent counselling about career pressure from disclosure of suicidal thoughts.

8. Abuse disclosures (POCSO). A disclosure of sexual abuse by a minor goes to a trained human reporter, who files with the police or the Special Juvenile Police Unit, not to a parent. Do not substitute a private inquiry or verify the child's account first. Good-faith reporting is protected. Confirm s.19 and s.21 against India Code.

9. No police or school reflex for attempts, and no legal guarantees. MHCA s.115 frames an attempt as a matter of care, not criminality, so there is no statutory basis for routing attempts to police or school discipline. Say that telling the counsellor is about care, not punishment. Never assure a student that 'nothing will happen to you legally', because the s.115 presumption is rebuttable and courts have debated its reach. Confirm the text against India Code.

10. Never-do list. Never give method, means or lethality information, with a hard-coded refusal at every risk tier and specific testing of the intermediate-risk band. Never encourage, instruct or facilitate self-harm, which is the abetment exposure under BNS s.107. Never coach secrecy or push a minor to hide thoughts from trusted adults. Never act as therapist. Never let safeguards degrade over a long session. Test in Hindi and Hinglish, since behaviour there is unmeasured.

11. Consent and data. Build to the DPDP 2027 standard now: verifiable parental consent before processing a child's data, and a Rule 10 check that the claimed parent is an adult. Limit safety detection to the minimum necessary, and never reuse it for profiling, marketing or behavioural tracking. Treat s.7(f) as an emergency-only basis that is untested for AI chat. Counsel must resolve s.9(3) and the Fourth Schedule before launch. Verify the Schedule text against the Gazette.

12. Age assurance. A self-declared birthday is not enough. Where age is uncertain, default to the safer, minor-grade experience. Weak age assurance has drawn regulatory fines. [unverified support: 29, 30, 31 for the US statutory benchmarks]

13. Logging and retention. Log every flag, the action taken, the timing and the human response, because the log is both the safety record and the evidence of what the operator knew. Retention period, access list, third-party LLM, speech-to-text and cloud vendors, cross-border transfer, erasure duties and litigation hold are an open gap that no finding resolved. Counsel must set them before launch.

14. Governance and shields. Treat the operator as a first-party publisher of the bot's outputs and do not assume s.79 safe harbour. Do not rely on disclaimers or click-through terms for a minor, since Indian law treats a minor's contract as void and US courts have declined to treat chatbot output as protected speech. Publish the escalation protocol, appoint a clinical-safety owner, train staff on psychological first aid at least twice a year as the Sukdeb Saha benchmark suggests, and run multi-turn crisis evals. [unverified support: 45, 29]

selfReview.weakest_claim: The headline premise that safest help and minimum liability are served by the same design, together with the claim that "detection creates the duty". It rests mainly on Raine, which the briefing itself calls allegations. It also rests on Sukdeb Saha, which the briefing admits binds schools and coaching centres and not a private AI operator, and which no lens read in full. The result is that the central "log it, route it, name a human" prescription is justified by analogy and by pleadings, not by any holding. Inside that, the POCSO point is the most likely wrong. The briefing says a human reading a transcript fixes "knowledge" and attaches the duty. But the s.19 duty arises when a person has "knowledge" or "apprehension" that an offence is likely, and the s.21 liability for the person in charge of a company or institution is read from non-official text. Reading the briefing's own argument, a design that triages for abuse at scale probably creates constructive knowledge at the company level when the classifier flags it, whether or not a human opens the transcript. So the "AI-only is unresolved" hedge may be understated, and the practical advice (route to a trained reporter) is right while the stated trigger is probably wrong. Other weak spots: the "Tele-MANAS 14416 as 24x7 multilingual default" line is unverified. "Removing minors is a product choice, not a legal requirement [38]" is supported only by "argument, not evidence". The T2 "ask a direct safety question" is labelled evidence-based, but the cited support is thin.)
selfReview.bias_check: There is a US-litigation and clinical-safety framing bias. Raine and the US cases supply the liability narrative even though the operator is Indian, so the plaintiff-side risk model (negligent failure to escalate) is imported and the Indian tort and consumer-protection routes are only gestured at. Four lenses citing the same Raine case, plus secondary summaries of Sukdeb Saha, give an echo-chamber reliability that the "High" labels do not reflect. Several findings are graded "High, T3" while their own caveats say the text is unread or non-official. That is grade inflation in the confidence labels. There is also a precautionary bias. Every ambiguous case is escalated to T2 or higher, and the briefing never prices the false-positive cost to students beyond one mention, even though it cites high false-positive rates itself. The rule set reads as prescriptive certainty (the Rule 7 T3 guardian override, for example) over evidence that is about adults and school settings. The briefing is also confident that disclaimers and terms fail for a minor, when a minor's contract being void does not decide whether duty-limiting notices or parental terms would work.)
selfReview.missing_perspective: The briefing is silent on or thin on five points. (1) A practising Indian lawyer and a regulator view: DPDP Board enforcement, the IT Act and Intermediary Rules, the consumer-protection route, and whether the operator's directors face personal exposure. (2) The clinician and crisis-line operators' view of what an AI-to-human handoff actually looks like at night, their capacity, and whether Tele-MANAS accepts warm transfers or third-party referral calls at all. (3) The adolescent and parent voice, especially the real Indian family dynamics where the parent is the pressure source. The rule on harmful parents says "escalate to a human to decide" and gives that human nothing to decide with. (4) The human counsellors' own exposure and welfare: vicarious trauma, indemnity cover, and whether a named on-call clinician is an employee or a contractor, since the stated aim is to minimise their liability. (5) The practical and commercial view: insurance (professional indemnity, cyber), contractual allocation with the LLM and speech vendors, and cost and feasibility for a small operator of a 24x7 clinician rota. Also missing: Indian-language and voice classifier recall figures, and any safe-messaging guidance from India's own bodies, since the cited guidance leans on WHO and Western sources.
